findings.title: Query-string array index sizes an unbounded slice allocation in the deepObject decoder

location.component: sliceMapToSlice, reached from urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject -> makeObject -> buildResObj

findings.evidence: Source-to-sink, all inside code in scope. Source: urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject, style deepObject (req_resp_decoder.go:661-686) walks every query parameter name, extracts the bracketed segments with `\[(.*?)\]` and joins them into a props key; the last segment of `?filter[ids][N]=x` becomes the map key "N", entirely attacker-chosen. makeObject (:911) splits that key and deepSet (:899) builds mobj = {"ids": {"N": "x"}}. buildResObj (:965) sees an array-typed property, takes the map branch at :976-981 and calls sliceMapToSlice (:936). There, every key is parsed with strconv.Atoi (:941) - which accepts any int64 - and the maximum is taken at :947-951 with no comparison against anything the client does not control. The sink is the loop at :953: `for i := 0; i <= max; i++ { result = append(result, ...) }`, followed by a second allocation of the same size at :986, `resultArr := make([]any, len(arr))`. A request of the form `GET /x?filter[ids][2000000000]=1` therefore asks the process to materialise ~2e9 interface values (16 bytes each on 64-bit) from about thirty bytes on the wire. Negative indices are harmless (max stays -1), large positive ones are not.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated client - authenticated only where the operation declares a security requirement - drives the server process into memory exhaustion and OOM termination with a single short request, and can repeat it. This is an availability compromise of the whole host process, not of one request: the allocation happens in the decoder, before any schema constraint is evaluated.
findings.preconditions: The document declares an object-typed parameter with style deepObject that contains (directly or nested) an array-typed property, and requests reach openapi3filter.ValidateRequest / ValidateParameter. No authentication is needed when the operation, or the document, declares no security requirement.
findings.recommendation: Bound the reconstruction of an array from indices before it allocates: reject in sliceMapToSlice any index above a configurable maximum (and above len(m) plus a small slack, since a dense array cannot have more elements than it has keys), and build the result by iterating the keys actually present rather than counting from 0 to max. The schema's own maxItems must not be relied on for this - it is only read later, in Schema.visitJSONArray, once the slice already exists.
findings.limits: No runtime reproduction was possible: the audit host has no Go toolchain, so the allocation was not measured, only read. The finding does not establish the exact index at which a given deployment dies - that depends on available memory and on GOMEMLIMIT - and it does not establish behaviour for consumers who replace the decoder.

findings.title: Legacy router panics on any request whose HTTP method is not one of the nine standard ones
findings.evidence: openapi3/path_item.go:153-176 - GetOperation switches on the nine methods of net/http and its default branch is `panic(fmt.Errorf("unsupported HTTP method %q", method))`. routers/legacy/router.go:109 takes `method := req.Method` verbatim from the request; net/http accepts any RFC 7230 token as a method, so this is an arbitrary attacker-supplied string. Line 141 asks the pathpattern trie for `method + " " + remainingPath`; the trie was built in NewRouter (:66-71) only from the methods returned by PathItem.Operations(), which are the nine standard ones upper-cased, so an unknown method never matches and node is nil. Line 148 then falls back to an exact map lookup, `doc.Paths.Value(remainingPath)`, which succeeds for any literal declared path such as /health or /users, and line 150 calls pathItem.GetOperation(method) with the attacker's token, reaching the panic. A lower-case standard method ('get') takes the same route, because the trie holds only the upper-cased form. Line 158 of the same fall-through would then dereference `node.VariableNames` on the nil node if GetOperation ever returned instead of panicking.
findings.impact: Any client can crash the request goroutine with `curl -X PROPFIND https://host/<declared-path>`. Under net/http the panic is recovered per connection, so the effect is a 500, a dropped connection and a full stack trace written to the server error log on every attempt - a cheap log-flooding and internal-path-disclosure primitive. Where the router is driven outside an http.Server's recover (a worker goroutine, a Lambda-style handler, a gateway with its own dispatch loop), the same request terminates the process.
findings.preconditions: The consumer uses routers/legacy (it is the router that openapi3filter.ValidationHandler installs by default, validation_handler.go:39), and the request path equals a declared path literally. No authentication is required: routing happens before any security requirement is evaluated.
findings.recommendation: Make GetOperation total - return nil for an unrecognised method instead of panicking - and add the nil-node guard at routers/legacy/router.go:158 so the fall-through returns routers.ErrMethodNotAllowed rather than continuing. A parser reached by network input must not use panic as its error channel.

triage.reason: net/http's per-connection recover is not this rule: it bounds the blast radius after the fact, it is not a control on the path to the sink, and it is absent in every deployment that drives the router outside an http.Server handler goroutine.

findings.limits: Not reproduced at runtime (no Go toolchain on the audit host). The finding does not establish process death for consumers running behind net/http, whose conn.serve recovers handler panics; it establishes the panic and names the deployments where recovery is absent. The gorillamux router is not affected: its mux route restricts the method set before GetOperation is reached (routers/gorillamux/router.go:72,116).

findings.title: Request decoder dereferences five schema pointers that the document is allowed to omit
findings.evidence:
The decoder assumes schema fields that the document validator treats as optional, in five places, each reachable by a request.
(a) A parameter declared with `content:` but no `schema:` is accepted by openapi3/media_type.go:125 - `if schema := mediaType.Schema; schema != nil` - so nothing rejects it. req_resp_decoder.go:195 then does `outSchema = mt.Schema.Value` with no guard, and decodeContentParameter only reaches it once the client actually supplies the parameter (:145-149 returns early when it is absent). This one is version-independent: `content: {application/json: {}}` on any 3.x document is enough.
(b)-(e) openapi3/schema.go:1690 makes `items` optional whenever jsonSchema2020ValidationEnabled is set, and openapi3/openapi3.go:268-271 with validation_options.go:39-42 sets it automatically for every document at 3.1 or later, so `type: array` with no `items` passes doc.Validate(). Four decoder sites then dereference the missing SchemaRef: :1398 `items := propSchema.Value.Items.Value` (any request with Content-Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded whose body schema has such a property); :1106 and :555 pass `schemaRef.Value.Items` (nil) into parsePrimitive, whose first statement, at :1128, is `schema.Value.Type.Slice()`; and :1541 assigns the nil Items to valueSchema before handing it to decodeBody and then to parsePrimitive at :1556. Each is a nil pointer dereference.
findings.impact: A client turns a well-formed request into a runtime panic. Under net/http the panic is recovered, so the observable result is a 500 with a stack trace in the log instead of the 400 the caller should have received; outside an http.Server's recover it terminates the process. In the urlencoded case the panic is unconditional for that operation, so the endpoint is unusable for every client, not only the attacker.
findings.preconditions: Either (a) any operation declares a parameter with `content` and no `schema` - no version constraint - or (b) the document is OpenAPI 3.1 or later and declares an array with no `items` on a parameter or on a request-body property. In both cases a request that supplies the parameter or the body reaches the dereference. Documents at 3.0.x are not affected by (b): Validate rejects an array without items there.
findings.recommendation: Guard every one of the five sites and treat the absent pointer as 'no constraint' rather than as a value: return the parameter undecoded when a content-typed parameter has no schema, accept the raw string when an array has no items, and give parsePrimitive an explicit nil-schema branch instead of dereferencing its argument. The root cause is a mismatch between what Validate accepts and what the decoder assumes, so a test that decodes against each optional-field shape belongs with the fix.

triage.reason: Same reading as F-002: the only thing standing between the dereference and process death is the caller's recover, which is not a control the library enforces and which several deployment shapes do not provide.

findings.limits: Not reproduced at runtime (no Go toolchain on the audit host). The finding does not establish that any real deployment ships such a schema - it establishes that the library accepts these shapes as valid and then cannot decode against them. Both preconditions were traced in the validator as well as the decoder. The response side, which was not read, may contain further sites of the same class.

findings.title: Request bodies are buffered and decoded with no size limit, and the pre-authentication read has none either
findings.evidence: validate_request.go:271 - `data, err = io.ReadAll(req.Body)` with no wrapping MaxBytesReader and no configurable cap; the same unbounded read appears at :448 inside validateSecurityRequirement, which runs before the AuthenticationFunc is called, so the whole body is resident in memory before the request is known to be authenticated. The buffered bytes are then handed to decodeBody (:324) and, for the default JSON media types, to JSONBodyDecoder (req_resp_decoder.go:1361) which decodes into an `any` tree: a body of repeated small JSON scalars expands into interface headers, json.Number strings and map buckets many times the size of the wire representation, so the peak is a multiple of the bytes sent. openapi3filter/options.go declares no limit of any kind, and grep over the tree finds no MaxBytesReader, no LimitReader and no Max*Size knob in the request path. Neither middleware wraps the body either (middleware.go:114-133, validation_handler.go:76-107).
findings.impact: Concurrent clients hold an unbounded and amplified amount of server memory. Because the read in validateSecurityRequirement precedes authentication, an operation that requires credentials still buffers the attacker's body in full before rejecting them, so the cost cannot be shed by the auth layer the library itself invokes.
findings.preconditions: The consumer does not itself wrap r.Body with http.MaxBytesReader or an equivalent before the validator runs, and does not front the service with a proxy that caps the body.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit maximum to Options (bytes, default off for compatibility but documented as strongly recommended) and enforce it with io.LimitReader/http.MaxBytesReader at both read sites; enforce it in validateSecurityRequirement first, so the pre-authentication read is the smallest one. Document in the README that the caller must cap the body when it does not set the option.

triage.reason: Whether a limit exists in front of the library - an ingress proxy-body-size, an API gateway, a WAF - is a property of each consumer's deployment and no such artifact exists inside this repository. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS.
The construct is what it looks like: io.ReadAll over an http.Request body, with no wrapper between the server and the call at either site.

findings.limits: One triage rule is UNKNOWN, so this finding is reported at the strength the evidence supports and not as an exploited case; the amplification factor of the JSON decoder was reasoned about rather than measured, because no Go toolchain was available. The finding does not claim that any particular deployment is unprotected - it claims the library provides no bound and no knob.
findings.inference: That no layer in front of the library caps the request body in the deployments that use it. The absence of any limit inside the library is observed; whether an ingress, gateway or WAF supplies one is a property of each consumer's environment and cannot be read from this repository.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The ingress or gateway configuration of a consuming deployment - an nginx proxy-body-size, an ALB or API-Gateway payload limit, or an http.MaxBytesReader wrapper in the consumer's handler chain. Any one of those, exported, turns the inference into an observation in either direction.

findings.title: ValidationHandler silently replaces a missing AuthenticationFunc with one that approves everything
findings.evidence: The core validator fails closed: validate_request.go:431-433 returns ErrAuthenticationServiceMissing when Options.AuthenticationFunc is nil, so a consumer who forgets to supply one gets an error on every request. ValidationHandler.Load reverses that at validation_handler.go:47-49 - `if h.AuthenticationFunc == nil { h.AuthenticationFunc = NoopAuthenticationFunc }` - and NoopAuthenticationFunc (:18) is `return nil`, i.e. every security scheme of every operation is declared satisfied. That value is then handed straight to Options.AuthenticationFunc at validation_handler.go:92. Load returns no error and logs nothing. The struct field carries no warning comment, and the README contains no occurrence of 'AuthenticationFunc', 'security' or 'Noop' at all, so nothing in the repository tells the caller that the default is permissive.
findings.impact: A service that mounts ValidationHandler and relies on it to enforce the security requirements declared in its own OpenAPI document enforces nothing: every request is treated as satisfying every declared scheme, and the failure is silent at construction time and at request time. Whether an unauthenticated caller actually reaches protected functionality then depends on whether the wrapped handler performs its own check.
findings.preconditions: The consumer uses openapi3filter.ValidationHandler (rather than calling ValidateRequest with explicit Options) and does not set AuthenticationFunc.
findings.recommendation: Make Load return an error when AuthenticationFunc is nil and the document declares any security requirement, so the insecure configuration cannot be reached by omission; keep NoopAuthenticationFunc as an explicit opt-in. Until then, document the default at the field and in the README.

triage.reason: There is no layer that cannot be skipped: the substitution happens inside the only component that would have enforced the requirement, and whether the wrapped handler re-checks is the consumer's choice, which is exactly the 'control a caller may forget' that FP-01 excludes.
This is an insecure default rather than a tainted value; nothing attacker-controlled flows into a sink here.
The second principal is an unauthenticated remote client of the consumer's API; the boundary crossed is the API's declared security requirement.

findings.limits: This establishes an insecure-by-default construction path in a published library, not an exploited application. Whether any given consumer is exposed depends on whether its own handler authenticates independently; that is outside this scope.

findings.title: CI job exports GITHUB_TOKEN to every step and declares no permissions block while building untrusted pull-request code
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/go.yml has no `permissions:` key at workflow or job level, so the job receives whatever the repository or organisation sets as the default GITHUB_TOKEN scope. Line 8-13 puts the token in the job-level env block - `GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` - which places it in the environment of every subsequent step, including the ones that execute contributor-supplied code checked out at line 36: `go generate ./...` (:38), `./maps.sh` (:41), `./docs.sh` (:44) and `go test ./...` (:56 and following). The trigger is `pull_request` (:3), not pull_request_target, which is the safe choice and is why this is rated as it is rather than higher.
findings.impact: Code proposed by a contributor runs in the same process environment as the workflow token. For pull requests opened from forks GitHub downgrades that token to read-only, which bounds the damage to reading; for branches inside the repository and for push events the token carries the repository default, and if that default is the permissive read-write set the executed test code can use it against the repository's own API surface.
findings.preconditions: A pull request or push whose code reaches one of the execution steps. The severity of the outcome depends on the repository's effective default token permissions, which are set outside the tree.
findings.recommendation: Add `permissions: contents: read` at workflow level and grant more only to the specific job that needs it; remove GITHUB_TOKEN from the job-level env block and pass it as a step-level env only to the steps that genuinely need an authenticated API call (none of the current steps obviously does).
findings.inference: The effective default GITHUB_TOKEN permission set for this repository and its organisation. With no permissions block in the tree, the scope actually granted at run time cannot be read from the repository, so the size of the exposure is inferred rather than observed.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The repository's Settings - Actions - General - Workflow permissions value (or the organisation policy that pins it), exported as an artifact; equivalently, the `permissions` object of any recent workflow run's job log.

triage.reason: The second principal is any outside contributor who can open a pull request against a public repository; the boundary crossed is between unreviewed code and the workflow's credential environment.

The compensating control - an organisation-level ruleset that pins default workflow permissions to read-only - would live outside the repository, and no exported artifact for it is in scope. Per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN, which is why the status is probable and not confirmed.

findings.limits: This does not establish that the token is currently write-scoped, and it does not establish that a fork PR can exfiltrate it - GitHub's fork downgrade makes that unlikely on the pull_request trigger. What it establishes is that the workflow relies entirely on a setting it does not declare.

findings.title: CI runs third-party actions pinned only by tag and executes four Go tools resolved at @latest
findings.evidence: Mutable references executed by the pipeline: go.yml uses actions/setup-go@v6 (:27), actions/cache@v3 (:31) and actions/checkout@v6 (:36 and :143); shellcheck.yml uses actions/checkout@v2 (:11) and the third-party action ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0 (:13). A Git tag is movable, so none of these identifies an immutable artifact. Worse, four steps fetch and execute code resolved at build time: `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest -test -diff -fix ...` (:62, and note it runs with -fix, i.e. it is allowed to rewrite the tree), `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/nilness/cmd/nilness@latest ./...` (:87), `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` (:148) and `go run -a github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/cmd/validate@latest ...` (:129). @latest is resolved against the module proxy at run time, so the code executed on any given day is whatever the newest published version happens to be.
findings.impact: Compromise of any of those upstream repositories, of a maintainer account able to move a tag, or of a module publishing account, results in attacker-chosen code executing inside this project's CI with the workflow token in its environment (see F-006) and, for the modernize step, with permission to modify the checked-out source before the test and diff steps run.
findings.preconditions: Any workflow run. No action by an attacker against this repository is needed; the trust is delegated upstream.
findings.recommendation: Pin every action to a full commit SHA with the human-readable tag in a trailing comment, and enable Dependabot for github-actions so the pins are maintained. Replace each @latest with an explicit version (a tools.go / go.mod tool directive so the versions are locked and reviewable), and drop -fix from the modernize step so a CI tool cannot rewrite the tree it is checking.

triage.reason: The second principal is each upstream action author and Go module publisher, plus anyone who compromises those accounts; the boundary crossed is between their release process and this repository's build environment.

It is not defence-in-depth only: the workflow token is present in the same environment (go.yml:11) and the modernize step is invoked with -fix, so a compromised upstream reaches both a credential and the source tree rather than nothing.
No verification step stands between resolution and execution: there is no SHA pin, no checksum check and no allowlist in either workflow file.

findings.limits: This is a standing supply-chain exposure, not evidence that any of the referenced upstreams is currently malicious; no upstream artifact was fetched or inspected, because network use was out of scope for this engagement.

findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder appends the whole read buffer regardless of how many bytes were read
findings.evidence: The read loop at req_resp_decoder.go:1634-1646 captures the byte count as `n, err := rc.Read(buffer)` and then, at :1639, appends the entire fixed 256-byte buffer: `if 0 < n { content = append(content, buffer...) }`. The count n is never used. Every short read therefore contributes 256 bytes to the decoded value: the tail of the previous read is re-emitted as if it were file content, and the decoded string is longer than the archive's actual contents. The value produced here is what ValidateRequestBody then hands to Schema.VisitJSON, so the bytes that are validated are not the bytes that were uploaded. The same function carries its own warning about zip bombs in the doc comment at :1608-1609; that part is disclosed, this part is not.
findings.impact: For any consumer that registers this decoder, schema validation is performed against corrupted content - trailing garbage can make a value that should fail minLength/pattern/format checks pass, or vice versa - and the decoded string grows to a multiple of the archive's real size, adding an unnecessary memory factor on top of the documented decompression risk.
findings.preconditions: The consumer calls openapi3filter.RegisterBodyDecoder("application/zip", openapi3filter.ZipFileBodyDecoder) or equivalent. The decoder is exported but is not registered by the package's own init (:1334-1349, which registers fourteen other media types and not this one), so it is opt-in.
findings.recommendation: Append only the bytes read - `content = append(content, buffer[:n]...)` - and, while the function is being touched, bound both the number of entries and the total decompressed size against a configurable maximum so the documented zip-bomb caveat becomes an enforced limit rather than a comment.

triage.reason: The archive is the request body, entirely attacker-controlled, and the attacker also controls the entry sizes that determine how often a short read occurs.
The function is exported from the shipped package; it is not test scaffolding and is not behind a build tag. It is merely not registered by default.
The documented and intended caveat at :1608 covers decompression ratio only. The buffer-length defect is neither documented nor intended, so the intended-exposure rule does not absorb it.
The second principal is the remote client uploading the archive; the boundary crossed is between request content and the value the server validates and then trusts.

findings.limits: Not reproduced at runtime. The finding does not establish that any consumer registers this decoder, and it does not quantify how often archive/zip's reader returns a short read for a given archive - only that when it does, the surplus bytes are kept.

findings.title: deepObject decoding compiles two regular expressions per query parameter on every request
findings.evidence: req_resp_decoder.go:663-686 iterates over every key of url.Values and, inside the loop body, calls regexp.MustCompile twice: at :665 for `^<param>\[` and at :669 for `\[(.*?)\]`. Neither pattern depends on the loop variable in a way that prevents hoisting - the first depends only on the parameter name, the second on nothing at all - yet both are recompiled for each of the N query parameters, on each request, for each deepObject parameter the operation declares. Compilation, not matching, dominates: the work is O(N) regexp compilations where N is chosen by the client and is bounded only by the server's MaxHeaderBytes.
findings.impact: A single request carrying a large number of distinct query parameters converts a small amount of network traffic into a disproportionate amount of server CPU. It is an amplification factor on an existing surface rather than a new capability, which is why it is rated low.
findings.preconditions: The document declares at least one parameter with style deepObject, and the endpoint is reachable.
findings.recommendation: Compile `\[(.*?)\]` once into a package-level var, and build the parameter-prefix test without a regexp at all - `strings.HasPrefix(key, param+"[")` is exactly equivalent to `^<QuoteMeta(param)>\[` and needs no compilation.

triage.reason: Nothing caps the number of query parameters before this loop; Go's net/http limits the request line by MaxHeaderBytes only, which still permits tens of thousands of short keys.
The loop bound is len(url.Values), i.e. the number of query parameters the client chose to send.

This is not an absent defence-in-depth measure: it is a real cost multiplier on a live request path. It is rated low because the capability gained is marginal - CPU proportional to a request the client had to send anyway - not because the impact fails to reach the user.

findings.limits: Not measured: no Go toolchain was available, so the per-compilation cost is reasoned from the shape of the code rather than benchmarked. The finding does not claim a practical denial of service on its own.

findings.title: Enabling external $ref resolution grants a document arbitrary local file reads and arbitrary outbound HTTP with no allowlist or timeout

location.component: ReadFromHTTP and ReadFromFile behind DefaultReadFromURI, reached from Loader.readURL

findings.evidence: One boolean, Loader.IsExternalRefsAllowed, gates two very different capabilities. When it is set, resolvePath (loader.go:307-317, the absolute-path branch at :310) returns an absolute $ref path unchanged - `if filepath.IsAbs(componentPath.Path) { return componentPath }` - and otherwise joins it with path.Join against the document's directory, which resolves `../` upward without any containment check; ReadFromFile (loader_uri_reader.go:78-84) then calls os.ReadFile on the result, so `$ref: "/etc/passwd"` and `$ref: "../../../../etc/shadow"` are both honoured. The same flag admits ReadFromHTTP (:51-69), which issues a GET to any scheme/host in the $ref through http.DefaultClient - a client with no timeout and no host, scheme or address restriction - so `$ref: "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"` is fetched, its body is unmarshalled into the document, and a hostile or slow host can also hold the loading goroutine indefinitely. The library exposes no allowlist hook: the only override is ReadFromURIFunc, which replaces the whole reader, and the field comment at loader.go:39-48 notes that installing one also disables the IsExternalRefsAllowed check entirely. The in-tree consumer that turns the flag on is cmd/validate's --ext flag (cmd/validate/main.go:27), whose help text says only 'enables visiting other files' and mentions neither absolute paths nor network fetches.
findings.impact: A service or tool that resolves external references in documents it did not author lets the document's author read any file the process can read and reach any host the process can reach - the classic SSRF pivot to a cloud metadata endpoint or an internal service - with the fetched bytes ending up inside the parsed document and therefore inside whatever the tool prints, renders or stores.
findings.preconditions: IsExternalRefsAllowed is true (or a permissive ReadFromURIFunc is installed) and the document being loaded comes from a source the operator does not control - an uploaded spec, a spec fetched from a registry, a spec supplied on the command line by someone else.
findings.recommendation: Split the capability: separate flags (or an explicit policy object) for local-file refs and for network refs, with the local one confined to the document's root directory by default and the network one taking a scheme/host allowlist. Give ReadFromHTTP an http.Client with a timeout and a redirect policy instead of http.DefaultClient, and restate in cmd/validate's --ext help text that the flag also permits absolute-path reads and outbound requests.
findings.inference: That a consumer in the real deployment set enables the flag while processing documents from an untrusted author. Inside this repository the only consumer that enables it is cmd/validate behind an explicit --ext flag, so the untrusted-document half of the chain is argued rather than observed.
findings.what_would_settle_it: Any in-scope caller that sets Loader.IsExternalRefsAllowed = true (or installs a ReadFromURIFunc delegating to DefaultReadFromURI) on a document whose origin is not the operator's - for example a service handler in a consuming repository, or a documented cmd/validate workflow that runs --ext over downloaded specs.

triage.reason: The only control is the IsExternalRefsAllowed check itself (enforced at loader.go:118 and :348), which is the flag being turned on; once it is on there is no second layer, and installing a custom ReadFromURIFunc removes even that check.
The $ref string is a field of the document being parsed, so it is controlled by whoever authored that document; nothing constrains it to an allowlist before it reaches os.ReadFile or http.Client.Do.

findings.limits: This establishes what the capability is, not that a specific deployment exposes it: the flag is off by default and its two enforcement points are correct. No network request was made and no file outside the target tree was read during this audit.

findings.title: String validation dereferences a nil matcher when a pattern fails to compile and MultiError is enabled
findings.evidence: schema.go:2655-2680: the cache is consulted, and on a miss compilePattern is called. On a compile failure the error is returned only when multiError is off (`if !settings.multiError { return err }`); with multiError on the error is appended to the accumulator and execution continues to :2666, `if !cp.MatchString(value)`. compilePattern (schema_pattern.go:19-35) assigns the result of regexp.Compile straight into the RegexMatcher interface, so a failure leaves cp holding a typed nil *regexp.Regexp - an interface that is not nil and whose method call dereferences a nil receiver - and a custom RegexCompilerFunc returning (nil, err) leaves cp as an untyped nil interface. Either way :2666 panics rather than reporting the error it just recorded.
findings.impact: A panic during request validation instead of a validation error: a 500 and a logged stack trace under net/http, process termination where no recover is in place.
findings.preconditions: A schema whose pattern does not compile is reached at validation time with MultiError enabled. The normal flow prevents this - doc.Validate compiles every pattern at schema.go:1684-1687 and fails the document - so it needs one of: validation skipped, DisableSchemaPatternValidation set (cmd/validate exposes it as --patterns=false), or an openapi3filter Options.RegexCompiler that rejects a pattern the default engine accepted, which is not the compiler Validate used.
findings.recommendation: Return from the pattern branch as soon as compilation fails, in both the multiError and the single-error paths, instead of falling through to the matcher; and have compilePattern return an explicitly nil interface so a typed nil can never escape.
findings.inference: That a document carrying an uncompilable pattern actually reaches visitJSONString in a real configuration. The panic itself is read directly from the code; its reachability rests on the caller having skipped or reconfigured pattern validation.
findings.what_would_settle_it: A caller in scope that sets EnableMultiError together with DisableSchemaPatternValidation, or that passes an openapi3filter Options.RegexCompiler stricter than Go's regexp - either combination makes the fall-through observable.

triage.reason: doc.Validate is a compensating control for the default configuration (schema.go:1684), but it is not mandatory and the two documented options that disable it are exposed to callers, so it cannot be shown to cover every path to the sink.

Whether the pattern that fails to compile is authored by the operator or by an untrusted party depends on the consumer: in a request-validation deployment the document is the operator's, but in a spec-processing service it is not (see F-010). No in-scope consumer settles which it is, so this is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS, and the status stays at probable.
The branch is in the shipped library and is not behind a build tag or a test-only path.

findings.limits: One rule HOLDS and one is UNKNOWN, which is why this is probable and low rather than confirmed. The Go semantics that make the typed-nil interface non-nil were applied from the language specification, not demonstrated on this host.

findings.title: The global compiled-pattern cache is keyed by the pattern alone, so a custom regex compiler can be silently bypassed
findings.evidence: compilePattern stores its result with `compiledPatterns.Store(pattern, cp)` (schema_pattern.go:34) and the lookup at schema.go:2655 is `compiledPatterns.Load(schema.Pattern)`. Neither side records which compiler produced the entry, and compiledPatterns is a package-level sync.Map (schema.go:46) shared by every document, every Loader and every request in the process. Two consequences follow from the same line: a matcher compiled by the default Go engine is returned to a caller that asked for a different one through SetSchemaRegexCompiler or openapi3filter Options.RegexCompiler, whenever any earlier document used the same pattern string; and the map has no bound and no eviction, so a long-lived process that loads many documents accumulates one entry per distinct pattern for its lifetime. The file's own header comment already flags a related race between writes to schema.Pattern and this cache.
findings.impact: A consumer that installs a stricter or safer regex engine - typically to add a matching timeout or to reject patterns that the default engine treats as valid - can have that choice ignored for any pattern another document compiled first, so the control silently degrades to the default engine. The unbounded growth is a slow memory leak in spec-hosting processes.
findings.preconditions: More than one document, or more than one compiler configuration, in a single process. The bypass needs a caller that actually sets a custom RegexCompilerFunc.
findings.recommendation: Key the cache by the pair (compiler identity, pattern) - or move it off the package level onto the Loader or the validation settings - and give it a bound with eviction so document volume cannot grow it without limit.
findings.inference: That a consumer sets a custom RegexCompilerFunc for a security purpose. The cache-key defect is read directly; the impact of the bypass depends on a caller configuration that is not present in this repository.
findings.what_would_settle_it: An in-scope caller of openapi3.SetSchemaRegexCompiler or openapi3filter Options.RegexCompiler, plus a second document sharing a pattern string with the first, which together make the wrong-matcher return observable.

triage.reason: No layer re-checks which compiler produced a cached matcher; the Load at schema.go:2655 is the only gate and it takes the pattern string alone.
No tainted value flows to a sink here. The defect is that the cache key omits the compiler identity, so the question this rule asks does not apply to it.
The construct is what it appears to be: a package-level sync.Map keyed by a bare string, with a Store on one side and a Load on the other.

findings.limits: Reported as a control-integrity and resource defect, not as an exploited path; no consumer in scope sets a custom compiler, so the bypass was reasoned rather than observed.

findings.title: Legacy Router.AddRoute stores the wrong value type, so FindRoute can return a nil route with a nil error
findings.evidence: NewRouter stores a *routers.Route in each trie node (router.go:66-71). AddRoute, an exported method, stores the *Router itself instead: `return router.node().Add(method+" "+path, router, nil)` (:95). FindRoute reads nodes back with a type assertion, `route, _ = node.Value.(*routers.Route)` (:143), which fails for such a node and leaves route nil. Execution then enters the `if route == nil` block at :145; when the path is also a declared path with that method - which is exactly the case after AddRoute overwrites a node NewRouter had already populated - neither early return fires, and the function reaches `return route, pathParams, nil` at :163 with route nil and err nil. Every documented caller then dereferences it: openapi3filter/middleware.go:122-133 treats a nil error as success and passes the nil Route into ValidateRequest, whose first statements are `route := input.Route; operation := route.Operation` (validate_request.go:40-41).
findings.impact: A route registered through the exported AddRoute API is silently destroyed and, from then on, every request matching it makes the validating middleware dereference a nil pointer - a panic per request on that endpoint rather than a validation result. The contract violation is the deeper problem: FindRoute promises that a nil error implies a usable route, and here it does not.
findings.preconditions: The consumer calls routers/legacy Router.AddRoute. Consumers that only use NewRouter are unaffected.
findings.recommendation: Store a *routers.Route in AddRoute as NewRouter does, and make FindRoute defensive at the same time: use the checked type assertion and return routers.ErrPathNotFound when it fails, and guard node against nil before reading node.VariableNames at :158 (the same guard F-002 needs).

triage.reason: AddRoute is an exported method of a shipped package, not test scaffolding.
The second principal is the remote client whose request reaches the broken route; the boundary crossed is between the request and a validator that panics instead of validating.
The value stored and the value asserted are two different concrete types in the same file, twenty-five lines apart; there is no reading under which they match.

findings.limits: Not reproduced at runtime. Whether any consumer calls AddRoute is outside this scope; the finding establishes that the exported method is both non-functional and capable of breaking the nil-error contract.

findings.title: An AWS access key ID is tracked in a vendored third-party spec fixture

location.component: vendored copy of the SendGrid OpenAPI document, used by openapi3/issue594_test.go

findings.evidence: A scan of all 1,667 non-.git files for the high-precision credential formats (the GitHub, Slack, GitLab and Anthropic token prefixes, the AWS access-key-identifier prefix and the PEM private-key header) returns exactly one hit: line 29766 of openapi3/testdata/oai_v3_stoplight.json contains a documentation example of an AWS pre-signed S3 URL whose X-Amz-Credential parameter carries an AWS access key ID, [REDACTED:secret], alongside X-Amz-Date=20170728T223936Z, X-Amz-Expires=3600 and a truncated X-Amz-Signature. openapi3/issue594_test.go:13 records the file's provenance: it is a verbatim copy of sendgrid/sendgrid-oai's oai_v3_stoplight.json, i.e. a third party's public API document, not material authored here. No other credential format from that set appears anywhere in the tree.
findings.impact: None reachable. An AWS access key ID is an identifier rather than a secret; the matching secret access key is not present, and the signature it accompanies expired 3600 seconds after 2017-07-28. What it grants is the identity of an AWS account belonging to a third party, which is recorded here so that a reader does not have to re-derive it and so that an automated secret scanner's alert on this repository has a known answer.
findings.preconditions: None. The string is in the working tree of any checkout.
findings.recommendation: Leave the fixture byte-identical - it is a regression fixture whose value depends on matching upstream exactly - and instead add an allowlist entry for this path in whatever secret scanner runs against the repository, so the known-benign hit does not mask a future real one. If the fixture is ever regenerated, redact the credential parameter at that time.

triage.reason: The value is not attacker-controlled and is not the project's: openapi3/issue594_test.go:13 traces the file to a public upstream document published by SendGrid, and the string is an account identifier inside an illustrative URL, not a credential this project issued or uses.

The data has no exploitable security value on its own: an AWS access key ID authenticates nothing without the corresponding secret access key, which is absent, and the pre-signed signature it appears with declares X-Amz-Expires=3600 against a 2017 date, so it is long dead. Recorded at severity informational rather than dropped, because a scanner will keep flagging it.

findings.limits: Establishes only what is in the working tree. Git history was excluded from scope by instruction and was not searched, so SUP-17 (secrets that survive in history after removal from HEAD) is not covered either way. No attempt was made to use the identifier against AWS, and none would have been in scope.

ruled_out.class: Nil dereference in openapi3filter error conversion (the shape recorded in the in-tree test named for GHSA-mmfr-pmjx-hw9w)
ruled_out.where: openapi3filter/validation_error_encoder.go:108 and :120 - both branches that read e.Parameter.In test e.Parameter != nil first, so a request-body ParseError (e.Parameter always nil) falls through to the generic 400 branch that follows. Checked by reading every branch of convertParseError and convertSchemaError; convertSchemaError's enum branch reads innerErr.Schema, which openapi3/schema.go:2080-2083 always populates.

ruled_out.class: External $ref resolution while IsExternalRefsAllowed is false (default)
ruled_out.where: openapi3/loader.go:118 and :348 - every path that turns a $ref into a URI read passes through loadSingleElementFromURI or resolveRefPath, and both call allowsExternalRefs when no custom ReadFromURIFunc is installed. The only other readURL call, at loader.go:467, re-reads a document path already resolved, so it opens no new location. Bound: enforcement was traced for the default reader only; a custom ReadFromURIFunc bypasses it by design and that is F-010.

ruled_out.class: Catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) in schema pattern and format validation
ruled_out.where: openapi3/schema_pattern.go:23 and openapi3/schema_formats.go:102-108 both compile with the standard library regexp, which is RE2 and runs in time linear in the input, so an attacker-supplied string cannot force exponential matching. Bound: this does not cover a consumer-supplied RegexCompilerFunc backed by a backtracking engine, which would reintroduce the class.

ruled_out.class: Route-matching divergence in routers/gorillamux allowing validation to be skipped
ruled_out.where: routers/gorillamux/router.go:97-124 was read end to end; FindRoute returns ErrPathNotFound when nothing matches, so a miss fails closed rather than passing an unvalidated request through. What could not be settled inside this scope is whether gorilla/mux's UseEncodedPath matching and the target server's own path normalisation agree on encoded separators - that needs the dependency's source, which was not in scope.

ruled_out.class: Command injection in the repository's shell scripts
ruled_out.where: docs.sh and maps.sh were read in full. Every expansion that reaches a command is quoted (docs.sh:8-9 `go doc -all ./"$pkgpath"` and `tee "$outdir/..."`), and maps.sh interpolates only literals defined at the top of the file into here-documents that are written to disk, never executed. The only unquoted expansion, `echo $pkgpath` at docs.sh:7, reaches no command.

ruled_out.class: Secrets committed to the working tree
ruled_out.where: The high-precision credential formats - the GitHub, Slack, GitLab and Anthropic token prefixes, the AWS access-key-identifier prefix and the PEM private-key header - were searched across all 1,667 non-.git files. One hit, reported as F-014: an AWS access key ID inside a vendored third-party spec fixture. No project credential, no private key and no token belonging to this repository was found; the workflows reference secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN by expression rather than by value. Bound: the working tree only - git history was excluded from scope by instruction and was not searched.

Consulting an advisory database was forbidden for this engagement and no Go toolchain is present, so neither govulncheck nor a manual advisory lookup could run. The manifest was read for shape only: seven direct dependencies, all pinned to exact versions with checksums in go.sum, no replace directives and no local or VCS-pointer requirements. No claim is made about whether any pinned version carries a known vulnerability.

ruled_out.class: Response validation, document conversion (openapi2conv / openapi3conv) and openapi3gen
ruled_out.where: Inventoried and deliberately left unread in favour of the request path, which is the surface reached by untrusted traffic. These are listed in engagement.coverage.not_read; silence about them is silence, not a clean bill.
